content: This article discusses the treatment of influenza in humans, specifically focusing on mild cases of the flu. It includes approaches to alleviate symptoms as well as treatments targeting the influenza virus itself. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises flu patients to get adequate rest, consume plenty of fluids, and avoid the use of alcohol and tobacco. Antiviral Drugs Antiviral medications are treatments that directly target the influenza virus. These drugs can be used either prophylactically (to prevent infection) or therapeutically (to treat an active infection). For optimal effectiveness, antiviral drugs for influenza must be administered within a few days of symptom onset. During the 2005–2006 flu season in the United States, there was a significant increase in resistance to the antiviral drugs amantadine and rimantadine in H3N2 influenza strains. As a result, the CDC recommended the use of oseltamivir for flu prevention and either oseltamivir or zanamivir for flu treatment. Approved Antiviral Drugs Certain prescription antiviral drugs have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as both safe and effective for treating influenza. Experimental Antiviral Drugs Peramivir, an experimental antiviral drug developed by BioCryst Pharmaceuticals, is still under development and has not yet been approved for sale in the United States. Conventional Symptomatic Relief Over-the-counter medications can be used to alleviate flu symptoms, but they do not have any effect on the influenza virus itself. It is important to note that children and teenagers with flu symptoms, particularly those experiencing fever, should avoid taking aspirin. The use of aspirin in the presence of an influenza infection, especially Influenza B, can lead to Reye's syndrome, a rare but potentially fatal condition affecting the liver. Unconventional Treatments Homeopathic remedies and other cold and flu treatments that do not meet regulatory standards for being marketed as drugs or fail to adhere to evidence-based medicine standards are widely sold as nutritional supplements. These products are often heavily marketed and may be derived from extracts of living organisms. However, they frequently lack sufficient documentation regarding their safety and efficacy.
